not_covered_review.scope: NOT-COVERED review. 10 claims the LIVE judge (prompt 5b9090d7a60ce5d1) marked not covered in ALL TEN judged sessions on this document — the 4 PRIMARY sessions of era 1 plus d33800bf, bb979045, 6e9d58c5, 5004cb13, 9a2d38d0, 0ca94682, 9aa3ad47. Sampled from the 42 never-covered claims, deliberately mixed between genuine judgment calls and controls expected to be easy.
not_covered_review.why: Era 1 labelled only claims the judge marked COVERED, so the eval could catch the judge getting looser and was structurally blind to it getting stricter — a false negative under-fills the bar and reads to a tester as no progress. These rows are the not-covered half of the answer key, so the eval can fail in both directions.
not_covered_review.method_note: matt_verdict is ground truth; judge_verdict is the live prompt's call. confidence is 'transcript-verified' for all ten: every claim was checked against ALL 625 turns across all ten sessions. c45 was verified by READING every turn, not by keyword search, after Matt recalled it coming up — the recollection traced to a Mike Krieger mention that is evidence for c62, not for c45. not_covered_review.coverage_rule_v1: WAS THE CLAIM EXPLAINED? The test judges the TUTOR's output. There is no student-engagement term — whether the student took the topic up is not part of it — and delivery framing is irrelevant. Mentioning is not explaining.

labels.note: The tutor RECITED both clauses verbatim in its first substantive turn and handed them back as a question ('what do you make of that framing?'), then never unpacked what an anchor is or why verifying against reality differs from verifying against other model outputs. Headline, not lesson. `anchor` appears in only two other turns, both sign-offs promising the section 'next time'. This claim SETS THE v1 RULE: mentioning is not explaining.

Nodes, edges, bounded jobs and the fake-edge test are all explained repeatedly. The claim's mechanism — that both carry CONTRACTS enforced by a schema, letting you swap nodes without breaking the graph — never appears. The single `schema` hit in ten sessions is about structured extraction to avoid context collapse, a different subject.

Compound claim. The skeleton half (fan-out/reduce/synthesize, and the job types it names) is explained well and often. The cost half — cheap models on boring nodes, the strong model only where judgment matters — never appears; the one cost-adjacent hit is 'cheap enough to use routinely', about the economics of parallelism, not model selection.
Control. The go-to-market kit is one of the document's three worked builds and none of it appears: zero hits for go-to-market, landing copy, launch posts, or buyer profiling.

THE SOLE FALSE NEGATIVE of this review, and a MANDATORY regression case for any judge-prompt v2: v2 must mark c31 COVERED. In 7beee170 turn 40 the tutor explained the human-gate principle AND both of its failure directions — approving every step kills the graph's value, too few gates leave irreversible actions unwatched — which is the claim's entire content. It arrived as an aside while answering a question about the limits of AI judgment, and the judge appears to have discounted it for that. Delivery framing is irrelevant; explanation is the whole test. NOTE THE ERA-1 ROW: under prompt 632b73a34b1a22b1 the judge marked c31 COVERED and it was upheld on a familiarity pass. The live prompt 5b9090d7a60ce5d1 REGRESSED on it.
Control. Zero hits for rule citations on review findings.

Control, and the most heavily verified row: all 625 turns were READ, not searched, because Matt recalled the topic coming up. No turn discusses role-based model selection in any phrasing. The recollection traced to the single Mike Krieger mention, which is evidence for c62 — this claim names Krieger, which is how the memory attached to it.

The ingredients are explained — the fake-edge test, loop versus graph. The claim states them as a DECISION RULE for whether a graph is warranted at all, and that framing returns zero hits across ten sessions ('two jobs', 'no edge between', 'warranted', 'just a loop').

The defining example of its shape, and a case the judge gets RIGHT — a v2 prompt must not lose it. The tutor named Sumner, 'a million lines of code from one language to another', and 'in two weeks', then explained a DIFFERENT point: that one-time migrations don't transfer to VoiceTutor. The example was used as evidence, not taught. The claim's own content — Zig→Rust, the CI test-suite gate, the token and cost figures — never appears. (Bun is named in four other turns, but in the false-independence/worktree discussion, never connected to this migration.)

Five words in a list — 'Mike Krieger converting Python to TypeScript' — and nothing else. None of the method the claim is actually about (165,000 lines, the weekend, hundreds of agents, eight phase gates, three adversarial review rounds, the output-diff check) appears anywhere in ten sessions. Not even a headline was stated.

THE LIVE PROMPT PASSES THAT REGRESSION CASE.
summary.cross_era_finding_c31_original_2026_08_0: The same prompt change REGRESSED on c31: covered under 632b73a34b1a22b1 (era 1, upheld by Matt), not covered under 5b9090d7a60ce5d1 (era 2, contradicted by Matt). Both flips are on the same session, 7beee170. The v1→live change traded a false positive for a false negative; a v2 prompt must hold c30 not-covered AND restore c31 covered at the same time.
summary.cross_era_finding_c31_amended_2026_08_07: AMENDED after a 7-run variance measurement on session 7beee170 (both prompts, same session, same model, temperature 0). The original finding above is UPHELD in substance — v2 did regress on c31 — but it described the regression as a clean flip, and it is not: it is a VARIANCE regression. Measured: v1 marks c31 covered 7/7 (perfectly stable, the correct answer); v2 marks it covered 3/7 (a coin flip that leans wrong). The interesting part is what else moved. v1 was DETERMINISTIC on this session — 12 covered, identical in all 7 runs, ZERO unstable claims. v2 is not: 3 of its claims flip (c31 3/7, c28 5/7, c9 6/7) and its per-run total ranges 9-11. All three unstable claims are era-1 COVERED rows, so the instability costs recall on claims v1 got right every time. The v1->v2 change therefore bought a correct and STABLE c30 (v1 7/7 covered = wrong; v2 0/7 = right, no flipping) at the price of introducing variance on three claims that were previously stable. A v3 must be judged on flip RATES over repeated runs, never on single verdicts — and note the product stores ONE run per session, so today a session's number varies by ~+/-1.5 claims (~2.4 points of the 63-claim bar) for reasons that have nothing to do with the session.
summary.cross_era_finding_c31_amendment_note: Why the original was imprecise, kept because the mistake is instructive: it rested on the single stored sidecar verdict. An intermediate 3-run check then produced [False, True, True] and briefly suggested the regression was not real at all — that reading was WRONG, and wrong in the same way: 3 samples of a 3/7 claim is not a measurement. Both errors have one cause, sampling an unstable claim too few times. This is the concrete case behind the repo rule that a single-run label disagreement is not evidence.
